title: Loose pieces drop off
summary: The first question to ask on every move, and why it finds so many tactics.

steps.title: The first question
steps.text:
Here is a question to ask every single move: **what is loose?**

Attacking a defended piece usually just offers a trade. Attacking a loose piece is a real threat, because there is no recapture waiting. Most tactics begin with a loose piece, even the fancy ones.

On this board @B has two loose pieces. You found them in the last lesson. One of them is already attacked.

ask.question: What can @W play here?
ask.answer: Rxd7. The bishop on @d7 is loose and the rook sees it down the open file, so it is simply free.

steps.prompt: Two almost identical positions. In one of them Nx@e5 wins a bishop for nothing.
steps.question: In the other position, why doesn't Nx@e5 win?

choices.text: A pawn stands on @d6, where it guards @e5. The bishop is no longer loose.
The knight can no longer reach @e5.
The bishop now attacks the knight, so it can take first.

steps.explain: One pawn moved one square. In the first position the bishop is loose and Nx@e5 is free. In the second, the pawn takes back on @e5 and it is only knight for bishop.

scaffold.prompt: First, the question. Tap every loose @B piece.

tempting.explain: Bx@b7 takes a bishop, but the rook takes back: an even trade. Worse, the rook on @b7 now guards @d7, so the knight that was loose is not loose any more.

reasons.question: Why does Rx@d7 win a piece?

choices.text: The knight on @d7 is loose, and the rook attacks it down the open file.
After Rx@d7, the rook forks two @B pieces.
@B can take back on @d7, but it costs them a rook.

hints: The knight on @d7 has no defender. What attacks it?
Your rook on @d1 looks straight up the file.
steps.explain: Loose piece, direct attack, free material. Notice what found the move: not a pattern you had memorised, but the question you asked first.

steps.prompt: Now the other half of the habit. Tap every loose @W piece.
steps.explain: The pawns on @b2 and @c2 have no protector. They are safe for now because nothing attacks them, but they are exactly what your opponent will be looking for. Your own loose pieces are their tactics.

steps.prompt: Back to the first position of this lesson, with @W to move.
steps.question: Nx@e5 also captures something. Why is it worse than Rx@d7?

choices.text: The pawn on @e5 is defended by the knight on @c6, so Nx@e5 Nx@e5 gives a knight for a pawn.
Nx@e5 is just as good. Both moves win material.
The pawn on @e5 is loose, but pawns are not worth taking.

steps.explain: Both moves capture. Only one captures something loose.
